questions.q: Unpolarised light passes through a polariser and then an analyser. According to Malus's law, what is the intensity of the emerging polarised light?
options: \(I = I_O \cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the axes of the two filters
\(I = I_O \cos^2\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the axes of the polariser and the analyser
\(I = I_O \sin^2\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the incident ray and the analyser
\(I = \tfrac{1}{2} I_O\) for any angle \(\theta\) between the two filters
questions.explanation: Malus's law gives the intensity of light emerging from the analyser as \(I = I_O \cos^2\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the axes of the polariser and the analyser. It is a cosine squared, not a cosine, and plane polarisation is a wave behaviour specific to transverse waves.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity \(I_O\) falls on a polariser, then on an analyser whose axis is at 60° to the polariser. Find the intensity of the emerging light as a percentage of the original \(I_O\).
questions.given: Unpolarised light intensity \(I_O\); analyser axis at \(\theta = 60^\circ\) to the polariser
working: First filter on unpolarised light passes exactly half: \(I_a = 0.5\,I_O\)
Apply Malus's law between polariser and analyser: \(I_b = I_a \cos^2\theta\)
questions.explanation: The first polariser drops unpolarised light to exactly one half (you do not use Malus's law on the first filter). Malus's law then applies between the polariser and analyser: \(\cos^2 60^\circ = 0.25\), giving \(0.5 \times 0.25 = 12.5\%\).

questions.q: In the photoelectric equation \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\), what does the work function \(W\) represent?
options: The maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron
The minimum energy required to remove the electron from the metal surface
The energy of the incident photon, equal to \(hf\)
The threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted
questions.explanation: In \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\), the work function \(W\) is the minimum energy required to remove the electron from the metal surface, \(hf\) is the energy of the incident photon, and \(E_{k\,\max}\) is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron. The work function is an energy, not a frequency.

questions.q: On a graph of maximum photoelectron kinetic energy versus frequency for several different metals, what is true of the lines?
options: Each metal gives a line with a different gradient equal to its own work function
The lines for all of the metals are parallel and have a gradient equal to Planck's constant
The lines all pass through the origin because \(E_{k\,\max} = hf\)
The gradient equals the threshold frequency, which is the same for every metal
questions.explanation: The lines for all of the metals are parallel and have a gradient equal to Planck's constant. Applying \(y = mx + b\) to \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\), the gradient is \(h\) (the same for every metal) while the differing work function \(W\) shifts the intercept.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 425 nm strikes a metal and a stopping voltage of 1.25 V is needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons. The photon energy is 2.92 eV. Calculate the work function \(W\) of the metal in eV.
questions.given: Photon energy \(hf = 2.92\,\text{eV}\); stopping voltage \(V_S = 1.25\,\text{V}\), so emitted electron energy \(E_{k\,\max} = 1.25\,\text{eV}\)
working: Use \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\), rearranged to \(W = hf - E_{k\,\max}\)
Since the stopping voltage is 1.25 V, the energy of the emitted electron is 1.25 eV
questions.explanation: From \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\): when the photon energy \(hf = 2.92\,\text{eV}\) gives electrons of energy 1.25 eV, the work function is \(W = 2.92 - 1.25 = 1.67\,\text{eV}\). The stopping voltage in volts equals the maximum kinetic energy in eV.

questions.q: What did the classical wave theory of light predict for black body radiation that experiment contradicted, an effect called the ultraviolet catastrophe?
options: That the radiation intensity would fall to zero as the wavelength decreased
That as the wavelength became shorter, the radiation intensity would increase without limit, approaching infinity in the ultraviolet
That black bodies would emit only discrete spectral lines, not a continuous spectrum
That the peak wavelength would shift to longer wavelengths as temperature increased
questions.explanation: The classical wave theory predicted that, as the wavelength became shorter, the radiation intensity would increase without limit, approaching infinity in the ultraviolet — violating conservation of energy. This was the ultraviolet catastrophe; the real curve peaks and falls back to zero, which Planck explained by quantising energy.

questions.q: A hotplate glows dark red, and the wavelength of its most intense light is 4.0 μm. Using Wien's law, calculate the surface temperature of the hotplate in kelvin.
questions.explanation: Rearranging Wien's law \(\lambda_{\max} T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{K m}\) gives \(T = b/\lambda_{\max} = 2.9\times10^{-3} / 4.0\times10^{-6} = 725\,\text{K}\). A longer peak wavelength means a cooler body — hotter is bluer.

questions.q: From memory: in the time dilation formula \(t = t_0\gamma\), what is the proper time \(t_0\), and why is the dilated time \(t\) always greater than \(t_0\)?
keyPoints: The proper time \(t_0\) is the time measured in a frame of reference where the two events occur at the same point in space — the clock's own reference frame.
Gamma (the Lorentz factor) is always greater than 1, so \(t = t_0\gamma\) is always greater than \(t_0\); the moving clock ticks slow.
'Proper' means property (the clock's own frame), not 'correct'.
questions.explanation: The proper time \(t_0\) is measured in the frame where the two events occur at the same point in space — the clock's own reference frame. Because the Lorentz factor gamma is always greater than 1, the dilated time \(t\) is always greater than \(t_0\), hence 'time dilation'.

questions.q: In the Rossi–Hall muon experiment, the Earth frame measures the journey taking 6.5 μs while the muons age only 0.7 μs, and the muon's proper half-life is 1.56 μs. Calculate the Lorentz factor gamma and the muon half-life measured in the Earth frame.
questions.given: Earth-frame time \(t = 6.5\,\mu\text{s}\); muon proper time \(t_0 = 0.7\,\mu\text{s}\); proper half-life \(= 1.56\,\mu\text{s}\)
questions.explanation: The proper time for the muon half-life is 1.56 microseconds in the muon's frame. The Lorentz factor is the ratio of journey times, \(\gamma = 6.5/0.7 = 9.29\). The half-life measured in the Earth reference frame is \(t_0\gamma = 1.56\,\mu\text{s} \times 9.29 \approx 14\,\mu\text{s}\), which is why so many muons survive the trip.

questions.q: Using the module's evidence-to-model map, which set of evidence forces the wave model of light specifically?
options: The black-body curve, the photoelectric effect, and Wien's law
Diffraction, interference (the double-slit dark fringes), and polarisation
The Michelson–Morley null result, the muons, and the atomic clocks
Relativistic momentum, mass-energy equivalence, and time dilation
questions.explanation: Diffraction, interference and polarisation force the wave model. The black-body curve and photoelectric effect force the quantum (photon) model; the Michelson–Morley null result, muons and atomic clocks force relativity. Mastering this map answers most reasoning questions in Module 7 on sight.

questions.q: From memory: state the unifying punchline of Module 7 — how does the same constant, the speed of light, both open the module and force its most radical consequence?
keyPoints: Maxwell calculated the speed of light from electromagnetism (\(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}\)) and concluded light is an electromagnetic wave; Hertz confirmed it.
The same constant speed of light becomes Einstein's first postulate (constant for every observer).
That constancy forces special relativity — time dilation, length contraction and mass-energy equivalence (E = mc²).
questions.explanation: The speed of light is the through-line: Maxwell predicted it from electromagnetism to show light is an EM wave, and its constancy for all observers (Einstein's first postulate) demolishes absolute time and space, giving special relativity.
